newsitem.title: USA: U.S. says firms lose millions due to EU banana code.
newsitem.headline: U.S. says firms lose millions due to EU banana code.

text.p: U.S. fruit companies have lost hundreds of millions of dollars in revenues due to a 1993 European Union regime on banana imports, a senior U.S. official said Tuesday.

The United States, along with Ecuador, Guatemala, Honduras and Mexico, has challenged the EU's banana regime at the World Trade Organization, where a panel is expected to rule on the dispute early in 1997.
The official said the EU had virtually snatched business away from U.S firms like Chiquita Brands International and Dole Food Corp. and handed it to European firms like Dublin-based Fyffes Plc.
"The United States banana distribution companies are among the big losers in this," the official, who asked not to be named, told reporters.
U.S. companies used to be the dominant banana suppliers in most European countries before Brussels set the new rules, which give preference to countries Africa, the Caribbean and the Pacific.
Since then, according to the United States, U.S. companies have lost as much as 50 percent of their previous share in the world's most coveted banana market.
The United States further argues that the 1993 regime has stunted growth in the European market, which had been growing at about 10 percent a year during the previous decade.
A study conducted earlier this year by a Canberra-based think tank said that EU consumers have to pay $2 billion a year due to higher banana prices caused by the regime.
In some cases, the U.S. official said, American firms have had to buy back import licenses from European distributors, a practice he likened to paying ransom.
The EU has defended the banana arrangement born from its 1992 customs union, arguing that it protects the fragile economies of former European colonies in the Caribbean, Africa and the Pacific.
Without those preferences, the Europeans say, tiny island nations like Dominica and St. Lucia would be devastated.
